length.text: Adults usually 3-4 m; record about 5.6 m

iucn.long: Listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List, with a decreasing population. That assessment was made before the 2024 split into four species, so it will need to be redone.

overview.text: The King Cobra is the world's longest venomous snake: a huge, alert elapid of the forests of South and Southeast Asia. Its scientific name *Ophiophagus* means snake-eater, and other snakes are indeed its main food. It is also the only snake known to build a nest for its eggs. In 2024 scientists split it into four species; SnakeList's page and map still cover the king cobra in the older, broad sense.

identification.text: A very long snake with smooth scales and a hood it spreads when alarmed. Adult colour depends on the region: pale olive in Malaysia, bronze-brown in eastern India, glossy black with pale crossbars in the Western Ghats, often with pale bands that converge towards the head.

identification.label: Young
identification.text: Hatchlings look very different: jet black with bright yellow or white crossbands, which fade as the snake grows.

size.label: Typical adults
size.text: Adults typically measure 3-4 m, and individuals rarely exceed about 4.25 m.

size.label: Largest record
size.text: The longest reliably reported specimen, caught in Thailand, measured about 5.6 m (18 ft 4 in).

variation.label: Regional
variation.text: Colour and banding differ from region to region. These differences, together with DNA, are part of why the king cobra is now divided into four species (see Taxonomy).

distribution.label: Native (broad sense)
distribution.text: From India and eastern Pakistan through Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Indochina and southern China to the Malay Peninsula, the Greater Sunda Islands and the Philippines.

distribution.label: After the 2024 split
distribution.text: *O. hannah* in the strict sense is the Northern King Cobra of eastern Pakistan, northern and eastern India, the Andaman Islands, Indo-Burma and Indochina south to central Thailand. The Sunda King Cobra (*O. bungarus*) lives on the Malay Peninsula, the Greater Sunda Islands and parts of the southern Philippines; the Western Ghats King Cobra (*O. kaalinga*) in south-western India; and the Luzon King Cobra (*O. salvatana*) on Luzon in the Philippines.

habitat.text: Mainly a forest snake: rainforest, bamboo thickets and mangrove swamps, often near streams and other water, from the lowlands up to about 2,000 m. It also turns up in plantations and farmland next to forest.

behaviour.text: Mostly seen hunting by day, though its activity varies with season and prey. When threatened it can raise about a third of its body off the ground and spread its hood.

diet.text: Almost entirely other snakes - including true cobras and, now and then, other king cobras - with monitor lizards taken occasionally.

reproduction.text: Lays eggs. The female gathers dead leaves into a mound using her body and tail, lays her eggs inside, and then stays nearby to guard the nest. Clutch sizes differ between reports, roughly 15 to over 20 eggs.

conservation.text: It needs large areas of forest. A 2012 review reported local declines of more than 80 percent in parts of its range. After the 2024 split, the new species have not yet been assessed separately.

taxonomy.text: Long treated as a single species, the king cobra was shown by a 2021 DNA study to consist of four lineages. A 2024 revision in the European Journal of Taxonomy named them: *O. hannah* (Northern), *O. bungarus* (Sunda, an old name brought back), and two new species, *O. kaalinga* (Western Ghats) and *O. salvatana* (Luzon).
Despite its name it is not a true cobra (genus *Naja*): it sits in its own genus and is more closely related to the mambas.

names: *Ophiophagus bungarus* (Schlegel, 1837) - now a separate species again
*Ophiophagus kaalinga* Das et al., 2024 - split off in 2024
*Ophiophagus salvatana* Das et al., 2024 - split off in 2024

funfacts.text: It is the only snake known to build a real nest: the mother rakes leaves into a pile for her eggs.
